utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mikulicic, the Chamber was informed that you would like to address the Chamber in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I would like to address with a couple of minutes, so I would -- please let me go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mikulicic, is the Markac Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Our next witness is Dr. Ivan Herman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I put on the record that the Prosecution had asked for another 24 hours to make submissions in relation to a matter raised by the Chamber and related to interviewing witnesses. The Chamber has granted the request for 24 hours, and expects, of course, then the filing to be made today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Herman. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence requires that you give a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Herman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, you will first be examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Herman.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When answering my questions, kindly bear in mind that our conversation is being interpreted into the official languages of this Tribunal and that the interpreters require some additional time than is the duration or pace of our conversation. Hence, I kindly ask you to answer slowly and to pause between questions and answers so as to enable the interpreters to do their work. First of all, for the needs of the transcript, can you state your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: My name is Ivan Herman. I am a medical doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for 3D00877 to be put on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, before you there are two screens. On the right-hand-side screen, you are about to see the document; and on the left-hand-side screen, you have the transcripts of these proceedings which you can use to pace your answers. You recall, Dr. Herman, having given a statement to General Markac's Defence in May this year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the last page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, you will see the last page which was signed. Could you please identify the signature?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: This is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, at the time of giving this statement, everything you said, as recorded in the statement, was it true and accurate to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It is accurate, according to what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read this document before appearing here as a witness?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I had that opportunity, and I re-read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I asked the same questions of you today that were put to you on the 18th of May this year, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge, I seek to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1910. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1910 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, in a few sentences can you tell me something about your profession and your role in the first days of the Homeland War in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I am a medical doctor. I worked in the Varazdin General Hospital. I used to be its director for a number of years, and currently I am a deputy director of the hospital. My role at the beginning of the war was to organise the medical support of the Special Police. I was a volunteer in the Police Special Unit in Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you describe your tasks? What did it include, this effort to organise the medical support of the Special Police of the Varazdin Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: To organise that medical support, we followed the examples of certain foreign military medical systems, comprising of mobile surgical teams, comprising a specialist surgeon, a specialist anesthesiologist, an anesthesiologist technician, assistant, a surgical assistant, and, if needed, an ambulance driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A medical team of such composition for the needs of the Special Police in Varazdin that was put together the way you just explained, can you tell us in what way was the medical team or medical service organised in other police administrations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: On Mr. Markac's request, we expanded the same type of organisation across all units; that is to say, the teams covered the area affected by war, as needed. The contact person within the organisation was Dr. Mihaljevic, who was in the centre in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was his role?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: He was a co-ordinator. He had all the information about the needs for such mobile medical teams, and he determined which centres were to send out those teams. One must bear in mind that we had to organise wartime medical services in all towns of Croatia, keeping in mind at the same time the regular health system and health-care, which was not supposed to be put in danger in terms of providing assistance to civilians because such mobile teams were put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, your teams, therefore, provided medical care to the units of the Special Police. You have already described the composition of such teams. In relation to the members of the Special Police, were there any people there whom you relied on in order to provide such medical care?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I have already mentioned that I was in frequent contact with Mr. Mihaljevic as well as with all the commanders, and, of course, the main commander, Mr. Mladen Markac, and his deputy, Mr. Sacic. They asked that we perform our work in a quality and professional fashion and to provide assistance to anyone in need, be it a wounded person or someone else who may require any sort of medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, briefly, please describe to us your role in the preparation for Operation Storm as well as during the course of its implementation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I had a dual role. Firstly, I was a volunteer with my special unit as a physician. My role there was to be at the front-line, where no surgical teams were available, as they had to be in the rear; easily accessible, but in a safe place so that they could play the role assigned to them, which was to assist and perform surgical interventions. I was a point of contact between the front-lines, where the injuries took place, and the mobile surgical teams. Since we had no nurses, I also had to perform that role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, I'm now referring to item 6 of your statement, which is now D1910, where you say that in Operation Storm you took part from the 23rd of July until the 11th of August, 1995. Can you tell us about these preparations and the very beginning of the operation from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: The preparations for Operation Storm were very thorough and professional. I am now referring exclusively to medical preparations, because I'm not an expert when it comes to other things. We knew where the locations were for the mobile surgical teams because the operation was carried out in difficult terrain, so we had to determine the points where these teams would be. We also had to work out possible transport of patients to the surgical teams because of difficult terrain and dangerous terrain which was also mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard much evidence about the beginning of Operation Storm on the 4th of August. What I'm about to ask you is the following: Where, exactly, were you on the first day of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I want to point out that I was at a place where I have never been before. It was Mount Velebit, an area called Golic or Opaljenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's close to Mali Alan, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Mali Alan was controlled by the enemy, and it was our task to reach Mali Alan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, Dr. Herman, that first day of Operation Storm and the launch of the operations toward Mali Alan, what kind of consequences did it have from the medical point of view?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We made assessments and we expected the enemy to provide strong resistance, so we were prepared for heavy losses and many injuries. When I had seen the terrain, I concluded that it was possible that soldiers could injure themselves due to difficult terrain, that is, because they could fall and injure themselves. The area was mountainous, there were forests. In a word, it was difficult terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A minute ago, you mentioned that the territory in front of the first lines, between you and the enemy, that is, was mined. Were there significant difficulties for your service with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Well, of course, when you can that you're moving through mined terrain, there is the problem of fear, but there was also a big problem for our pioneers to make sure that our unit could move through that mined terrain and get into enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During the events, you were also injured. Can you briefly describe to us what happened and what kind of injury that was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I had an accident because the commander had ordered me to provide services to two units, our unit from Varazdin and another from Split. The Split unit was in the direction of the Celavac Relay Station, and they didn't have a surgical team. I was older than they were and not in such physical shape, although I was in good shape. But due to my age, I wasn't at their level, so I was supposed to act on somewhat less forbidding terrain. But the first shell that hit us hit the Split unit, and I suffered from the blast. I fell, and I remember that the members of that unit provided first aid to me. But I came to quickly, although I was in an initial state of shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, on that first day of the operation, can you describe to us the dynamics of the advancement of the Special Police forces and your medical teams?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: The dynamics was fascinating. They advanced very fast, unexpectedly so, and it was difficult to keep up with them. As I said, the terrain was very forbidding, and I believe that the pace of advancement was as high as possible for infantry to advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From the medical point of view, how did the fighters from the Special Police cope with the physical aspect of the operation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I must say that three members of our unit were injured. One was shot through the lower leg, and the other two suffered injuries from shrapnel or stones, because you could get wounded not only by the shrapnel, itself, but also from pieces of rock flying around. And we first -- or, rather, I first evacuated those wounded from the front-line, and then in the rear I also asked for assistance, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Dr. Herman, whether there were difficulties with regard to logistical support? I'm especially referring to supplying food and drinking water.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: During the first hours of the operation, it was almost impossible to supply our units with water and food. It only became possible on the following day, once the road to Mali Alan was liberated, and I filled my vehicle with as much water as it could carry, and food, too. So this was our logistical support. But as I said, during the first hours it was next to impossible, so they only -- the soldiers -- or, rather, the unit members only had what they could carry themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, after piercing the first line of enemy defence, what was the direction of movement of your unit and your medical team?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Once we left the forests and the heavy terrain, we reached the first settlements, Sveti Rok, Ricice, and Lovinac. Those villages, I may say freely, were totally devastated. All houses were without roofs, but I remember one house which was in a somewhat better condition, and in it was the enemy staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Herman, who populated those villages before the commencement of the conflict in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Those villages were populated by Croats. They made up over 90 per cent of the population, but they were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The damage you saw, was it a consequence of the attacks during Operation Storm or something else?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: On those villages, the damage was inflicted much before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you saw those houses, you could see bushes growing in the houses or out of them. So I'm not an expert, but that is the consequence I drew -- conclusion I drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Dr. Herman, when you reached the road, where did you head to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: The men gathered there, and the direction of our subsequent movement was toward Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Moving toward Gracac on that road, can you tell us what you saw on that road?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I must say that I moved down the main road because I was in a vehicle. Apart from some craters that could be seen on the tarmac, the road was in fair condition, I dare say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While riding toward Gracac, did you see any abandoned equipment or any other facilities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: There was scattered military equipment, there were abandoned old vehicles, but we had orders not to touch anything because of possible booby-traps. We were especially warned not to touch abandoned radios or any similar equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Doctor, whether there really -- whether there actually were some incidents involving booby-traps in the areas where you passed through?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I only heard of such incidents, but I haven't seen them personally, so I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, when did you enter Gracac with your unit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It was around about noon on the third day of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like in Gracac? And when I'm asking that question, I'm interested in the houses and the infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: After the totally devastated villages we had passed through, once we entered Gracac we saw some buildings that had been hit, but not many. They were abandoned. I remember passing by a store with an inscription "No wine, no rakija, no flour." But the buildings were abandoned, yet not heavily damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that upon entering Gracac you found a hospital that had been used by the military and the local population. Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It was on the right side of the street, and there was an inscription on the building, "Medical Clinic." It was -- it had good supplies and the phones were still working, and I found large quantities of medical drugs that, as opposed to the ones we had, were still rather fresh and usable, and the provenance was France.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, when you entered Gracac, did you see any civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: There were some civilians. And as far as I remember, we had orders to take all civilians out of their buildings. I even spoke to some, asked them whether they needed assistance. But there were no major interventions, and I must say that I established good contact with them. They were mostly elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the Special Police enter civilian buildings for any reasons? Do you remember seeing anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I reiterate that we moved fast. We were in a sweep. In some buildings, there may have been some enemy soldiers left behind, but I cannot say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, that on that occasion, that is, upon your entry of Gracac, a member of the Special Police was injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Upon entering Gracac -- if you mean the explosive device, I think that happened on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: A man entered a house and activated an explosive device, the origin of which I can't tell. He was seriously injured and subsequently died of the consequences of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We stayed for the rest of the day and spent the night there, and then retreated to the outskirts. I couldn't give you the names -- the exact names of those places because I'm not that familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After Gracac, what was the direction of your movement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: After Gracac, on the third day of the operation, we entered the village of Mazin, which was also abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any damage or traces of any fire at Mazin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: At Mazin, there were no extensive damages or traces of fire. The village was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your movement towards Mazin and generally in the movements of your unit, did you have occasion to notice any individuals entering houses, looting, or setting houses on fire, or any other type of criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I cannot testify to that because I never saw any of it. I believe that was due to the pace of advancement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After Mazin, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: After Mazin, we went towards Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What do you recall concerning your arrival just outside and entering the town of Lapac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I entered Donji Lapac protected by the military armoured vehicle. I moved behind it in my off-road vehicle. In addition to the medical equipment, I also carried food and water used by the fighters in the quick advancement. We entered the location via a forest road which was constructed by the JNA next to a facility that was on the side of the road. We advanced as fast as an infantry unit could, and I followed them with my vehicle. Upon entering Lapac, we saw civilians pulling out of Lapac. They were joined by some military vehicles and at least two tanks that I could see. One of the tanks fired in the direction of the forest, and it was only our luck that none of us were injured on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did members of the Special Police open fire on that column which included the enemy tanks as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: They were forbidden to act because they were a part of a civilian column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the situation you found in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: When we entered Donji Lapac, the situation was satisfactory. We were accommodated in the houses where we intended to spend the night, because we slept out in the open in the course of the previous days in the forest. I didn't move much about. One could see that there had been combat. In my view, the retreating army set certain haystacks on fire, which appeared rather ominously because it creates a lot of smoke and one cannot clearly see what it is that is burning. There were also a few buildings which were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience, how would you describe the damage on the buildings in Donji Lapac after the Special Police entered it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I would say this was minor damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did your unit indeed stay in Lapac and spend the night in those houses, as you just said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: That day, in the afternoon, from the direction of Udbina, I believe, members of the Croatian armed forces arrived. It is then that the general celebrating began with much noise and shooting. Our commander decided to pull out from that area, as distantly as possible. And as far as I recall, I believe we went to Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once the units from Udbina entered Donji Lapac, could you see any consequences there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I have to say that this was a general outbreak of joy, albeit a bit strange with firing. To me, personally, this appears dangerous, and I didn't care to move much in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see any houses being set on fire during that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: As we were leaving, I could see that some buildings had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said you spent the night somewhere outside Donji Lapac. Where did you go the next day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: There are two locations, Gornji and Donji Lapac. We went further towards the Bosnian border, where there was certain operations and deployment of our forces, although I'm not an expert to tell you any more detail about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the course of the movement of your unit, what was your relationship to the civilians you came upon along that road?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We treated them fairly. I remember having found an elderly, abandoned, sick lady in a house. I personally provided medical care to her. She didn't recognise me, and she took me for a member of the Serb forces, judging by the characteristic greeting she used. I spoke with her. I introduced myself, and I said that I was a medical doctor. In the course of that conversation, I provided assistance and left some medication with her. I also undertook an obligation upon myself to bring some food to her, which I did. I received -- subsequently, I forwarded that information on, stating that there was an elderly, sick lady in the house which needed assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Concerning this topic, which is the relationship towards civilians and towards enemy soldiers, did the members of your unit ever receive any instructions concerning that from their commanders?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Basically, any order contained a provision in which it was stated that the civilians should be treated fairly and assisted until civilian authorities are established. It would then be the obligation of the police to issue them with Croatian documents. I had many contacts with civilians, and I can tell you that the treatment was very fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the members of your unit received certain written instructions by way of a brochure that was distributed to them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I do. All members of the medical services were particularly cautioned of the need to respect this Geneva Convention. We were also obliged by our medical oath to protect civilians. What I can tell you is that all of my work-mates behaved in a fully professional and responsible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For ease of reference, I wanted to point out Exhibit D533 for the Chamber's perusal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Having arrived in the proximity of the Bosnian border, what further instruction there was concerning the Varazdin Police Administration unit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We found the order to return to Varazdin a bit surprising. We were basically told that we were to go on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why was it surprising to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Personally, I expected that the whole thing would last longer. The assessment must have been that the people were over-tired and that they needed to be replaced by reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall on which day you started pulling back towards your base in Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say, but I believe it was on the 9th, although I'm not 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which route did you take on your return to Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Returning to Varazdin, we went via Udbina. My wish to return via the Plitvice Lakes came true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That means that you did not go through Gracac as you were returning again?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We went via Udbina, which was the shorter route. I must say, though, that I slept most of the way because I was extremely exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, after the conclusion of Operation Storm, in the course of which you have already explained your role, did you have any further role with the Special Police units in Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Any further obligations of mine were mostly of civilian nature. Among other things, we had to train the divers of the Special Police Unit, since I'm a specialist in that. We established scuba-diving teams which were assigned different specialty tasks. One of those tasks was to check the bed of the Plitvice Lakes because we had information that it had been mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in any terrain searches in the area of Knin and Gracac once Operation Storm was completed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, I was never in Knin after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, in the course of your duties, did you have an opportunity to get in touch or share the company of Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I attended several meetings where we received our tasks to organise the Medical Service. We were asked to organise it in a professional and responsible manner. I recall my first meeting with General Markac, when we were -- when we met for the first time at Mount Velebit. He asked me if I believed that surgical teams could be introduced into that area, giving the type of terrain. He believed that they could be quite efficient in such circumstances. However, my position was that it was not possible. I tried to dissuade him from doing that. He proved himself right, because finally they were fully effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What impression did you gain of Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I know General Markac as a top athlete before the war, and I believe he is a moral, honourable, and professional person. He is a patriot and a professional in his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your conversations with him, did you ever gain an impression or did he ever tell you that he has any sort of bias towards the people of other ethnicities, religions, et cetera? Did you ever notice any discriminatory views of his?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. He insisted that we provide medical assistance to one and all, irrespective of their religious, ethnic, or any other affiliation, including gender. He insisted that we provide the same type of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My last question, Dr. Herman: Yesterday, you told me that you recently visited the area where you were during Operation Storm as a tourist?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: For me, it was a shocking visit to Mali Alan. I went there with my family to show them where we waged war, and with my son-in-law, who is French. I was shocked to still see the yellow tapes bearing the sign "Mined." I could not believe that we actually traversed that territory, as it is being de-mined only now. I did know, though, that it was mined at the time, and I went there without the needed professional background. I was also alarmed because I realised that I brought my family into a dangerous area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Herman. This concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Any questions by the Cermak and Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Herman?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Carrier. Mr. Carrier is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Herman. Just to deal a bit more about your background, you have been a member of the HDZ party since 1991, and previously you ran for political offices as an HDZ candidate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: An MP, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No. The question is: You've been a member of the HDZ since 1991, and you actually ran as a candidate on behalf of the HDZ on a previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I'm still a member of the HDZ. I used to be a member of the County Assembly and a part of the City Council of Varazdin. I'm currently the president of the Varazdin Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Dr. Herman, just to be clear, I noticed, when Mr. Mikulicic was asking you questions, that you tend to give more information than is required in the question, so if you could please just listen to the question and try to focus in on it. Mr -- or, sorry, Dr. Herman, you were interviewed --

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You were interviewed in May 2009. And when you were interviewed, Mr. Djurica Franjo was present. Mr. Franjo was the deputy chief and then later on the chief of the Police Sector within the MUP in the 1990s. Did you know Mr. Franjo or who he was at the time that you were interviewed in May 2009?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know Djurica -- or, rather, I didn't know him before. As far as I understood, he was the one who brought the other gentleman to my office for the interview. I don't know his other positions or functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Herman, can you very briefly explain to the Court who initially approached you to become a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I was called up by Mr. Soljic, who asked me on the phone whether I was willing to testify before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Soljic before you gave your interview in May 2009, and did you know what his role was with the MUP during the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him as a member of the special unit from Zagreb or, to be more precise, Lucko, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And when he called you to see if you wanted to be a witness, at the time did you recognise that he, in fact, was a senior member of the Special Police, and did you have any knowledge of his relationship with General Markac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I know that the gentleman was his personal driver of General Markac when I met him. I don't know about any other roles of his because I never had direct contacts with him, personal contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, you said that you entered Donji Lapac on the 7th of August, 1995. And I think it's more clear now, after your testimony, but you said that your participation in Operation Storm ended on the 11th of August, 1995. I take it that from the 9th, there remained two days, the 9th, 10th, and 11th, you were travelling back towards Varazdin, during which time you said you slept most of the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. The operation was supposed to last until the 11th. I only slept for a couple of hours in the vehicle when we headed for Udbina, which I believe isn't strange because I was totally exhausted. And we returned on the 9th, although previously we were informed that we would have to act until the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So at paragraph 6 of your statement, when you said that you were engaged from the 23rd of July to the 11th of August, 1995, you meant the 9th of August, it ended? Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, no. Don't nail me down on the date because it's been many years, so I don't remember the exact dates. But in preparing for Operation Storm, we came in early, and I stayed at Sepurine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just following up on your last answer, Dr. Herman, in terms of not wanting to be nailed down on the dates, it's true, isn't it, that you're not really sure of the precise dates in which you were in different places; for instance, Mazin, or Gracac, or Donji Lapac? And just so you're clear, the reason I'm suggesting that is because during your testimony today, you've changed a bit from the statement you gave before. So is that fair, you're not really sure about the dates?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as for my statement, you must understand that I'm in this kind of situation for the first time. When I said "the second day," I'm not sure how you -- what you understood that to mean, but I stand by my statement in which the dates stated are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So to go through it a little bit, then, are you not standing by your words in court today; you're standing by the statement? Again, I'll give you an example: Today, you said that you entered Gracac, you thought, was on the third day of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: That was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So now I'm confused. Are you --

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: -- standing by your statement, or are you standing by your testimony, or is it fair that you're really not sure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Herman, you were asked a little bit about the injury you suffered when you were in the Velebit, and that was on the 5th of August, 1995. You said, at page 12 today, that you -- when you were injured, you came to and that you were in a state of shock. Did you actually lose consciousness at the time you suffered this injury on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't lose consciousness, but the blast hurled me away, and I was shocked by being so close to an explosion. I believe that anybody in my position would have been shocked. But shocked doesn't necessarily imply loss of consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I understand that. I just was curious about your description that you came to, and that was part of the reason why I asked whether you lost consciousness. Did this -- other than being in a state of shock, did you suffer any other injuries at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I suffered contusions because I fell on the ground. The lumbar part of my spine was injured, and my right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Herman, in your statement, at paragraph 9, you mentioned that as soon as you entered Donji Lapac on the 7th of August -- now you were informed that a Special Police member had sustained injuries as a result of an explosive device planted inside of a building, and although you attended the scene, this person had already died. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I was informed that there was a lethal injury. And when I arrived at the spot, I didn't find the person involved anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Can you explain paragraph 9 of your statement? And I'll read it to you verbatim. These are your words: "We entered Donji Lapac. As soon as I entered the place, I was informed that a member of the Special Police had been a victim of an explosive device planted in a building. And when I arrived there, he had, unfortunately, died from his wounds." What you're saying now is that you never actually went there and you never actually saw anybody injured; is that -- am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: You're trying to confuse me. I said that the person had died from the injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So you did go, and you saw him, and he was dead?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I found him dead. I was elsewhere, and then I returned to my tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'm clear on that now. Now, in terms of the timing of this, initially it was suggested to you that this happened in Gracac by Mr. Mikulicic, and then you thought it was the next day after Gracac, which would be -- would have been the 6th of August, 1995. But in your statement, you said you didn't enter Donji Lapac until the 7th of 1995 [sic], so I'm trying to figure out if you actually know where and when this happened.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It happened as described in my initial statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The person that was killed, was he a member of the Varazdin Special Police Unit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No. I don't remember to which unit he belonged, though. I think he was from someplace in Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And you obviously reported the death of this Special Police member on the 7th of August, 1995, in Donji Lapac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I personally didn't report it because it was outside the area of my activity. I was only involved as a consultant. They consulted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have Exhibit P614 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, this is a document dated 26 November 2001, which is an analysis of the Special Police concerning the progress made during Operation Storm. It was sent to the Chief of the Main Staff of the HV, General Cervenko, from the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please turn to page 24 in the English and 31 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, you'll see, at the top of the page in the B/C/S, there's a section headed "Medical Support in Operation Storm."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could turn the page in English, please, to page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And there, Dr. Herman, at the bottom of the page 31 in B/C/S, there's a list of the number of Special Police members killed, wounded, or injured during the first five days of Operation Storm. And on the 4th of August, there were 32 wounded, 6 injured, and 5 deaths. On the 5th of August, there were 12 wounded, 5 injured, and 1 death. On the 6th of August, there was 2 wounded, 3 injured, no registered deaths. The 7th of August, 7 injured, no registered deaths. 8th of August, 2 wounded, 6 injured, no registered deaths. And then it goes on, in the next page in B/C/S, to give totals. Dr. Herman, I'm just wondering if you can explain why there are no reported deaths of Special Police members on the 7th of August, 1995, in this report, despite your testimony to the contrary about you attending to somebody and finding them dead in Donji Lapac on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I did not write this report, so I don't know how it was compiled. I don't know under which heading this killed policeman can be found. Possibly due to the combat activities, somebody made a mistake. But I repeat that I didn't write this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just following up on that, reports from the Special Police concerning the taking of Donji Lapac on the 7th of August, 1995, sent to Deputy Sacic - and for reference that's D556 and P586 - those don't mention any reported deaths in Donji Lapac either. You didn't write those reports either, but I take it you have no explanation for why that's not reported there either?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I cannot explain that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time now. It's 10.30. This would be an appropriate time to stop before I move to the next section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please. Would you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I will be less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than an hour. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10.30 -- no, at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, I apologise for dealing with two small procedural matters which the Chamber would like to put on the record now. So if you'd just have some patience with us this morning. First of all, Mr. Mikulicic, no summary was read, but, at the same time, I noticed that this situation -- the public would understand what the testimony is about, because you covered most of it in eliciting oral testimony from the witness. So under those circumstances, the Chamber would not insist on reading a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And I must tell you, Your Honour, I prepared the summary and I simply overlooked it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that almost all of what is found in the written statement is covered in one way or another by the oral testimony of the witness, and therefore the public doesn't have to guess what this evidence is about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, a second matter is -- I'm addressing both the Markac Defence and the Prosecution. The Chamber is considering at this moment what to decide on your application to add a witness to the 65 ter list, Mr. Watts. And the Chamber noted that this matter was introduced, and therefore the first round was without knowledge of what exactly Mr. Watts would come and testify about. It appears that once the report has been produced, that then actually -- at least that's how we understand the Prosecution's response, that initially, in the first round, to say so, you were unaware of what it was about, whereas only in the second round you provided the report, and then there came rather substantial objections by the Prosecution. The Chamber later this morning would like to give a brief opportunity, and I'm thinking in terms of five to ten minutes, for the Markac Defence to respond to a matter which, unfortunately, was raised only in the second round, although the Prosecution is not blamed for it because earlier they had no knowledge of what the report would contain. And it might be a matter which we might want to consider when deciding this matter. So if you could please prepare -- and I know that it may come as a bit of a surprise, but looking at all this material the Chamber thinks that it would be assisted by another brief exchange of views, and I would like to hear that later today so that the Chamber doesn't have to wait for another three weeks to decide on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does Your Honour have in mind to respond orally or to submit an informal written submission on the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the Chamber would like to hear from you later today orally so that we can continue to consider the matter this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, these are matters which are not of specific interest for you. We'll now further focus on your testimony, and Mr. Carrier will continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, today you described, in a bit more detail, your role in making medical preparations for Operation Storm, and you said that you had a dual role. Is it fair to say, Dr. Herman, that you were not involved in planning the overall Special Police military operation that was conducted during Storm? And I'm talking about in terms of deployment of Special Police forces, method of artillery support, axis of attack, method of clearing the terrain, those types of things. You weren't involved in that; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These are professional issues in which I took no part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Herman, today, at page 11 in the draft transcript, lines 13 and 14, you mentioned that at the beginning of Operation Storm you found yourself in a place where you had never been before, and you said that was Mount Velebit. Is that fair; you'd never been to Mount Velebit before the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I was on Velebit, but Velebit is a very large mountain. I have never before been at our starting position. And let me explain about the axis of attack. We had been at the starting position, but I was not on the axis of our action --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you off. I just want to be clear. I just want to know if you had been there before. So if you're saying that specific spot, let me just follow up. Were you ever in the Velebit area before August 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And on page 22 of the draft transcript today, you mentioned that you had met General Markac for the first time on Mount Velebit. I just want to be clear when that was. Did you meet him for the first time in August 1995, when you were preparing to start Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We are again speaking about two things, about knowing somebody and meeting him in the war. We were also in Operation Maslenica. I took part in that, too. And the area -- or, rather, that area was very close to our starting point. I couldn't go any further because the mountain was held by the enemy, and the front-line was there. I hope we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. So specifically about Operation Storm, I'd like you to tell the Court, how much direct contact did you actually have with General Markac in the weeks leading up to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'll be more clear. So Operation Storm started on the 4th of August, 1995. During the two or three weeks leading up to that point, did you have any direct contact with General Markac during that period?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I don't remember. I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And what about during Operation Storm and following; did you have any direct contact with General Markac during that period? And if you could just give us the instances.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I saw him once in or around Mazin, but not later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: When you say you saw him once, you mean physically you saw him with your eyes? You didn't sit down and talk with him or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We were all there, the entire command, on that position, and we proceeded from there to the subsequent activities. So I saw him there and was in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: My question was whether you talked to him, sat down with him, had direct communication with him.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. At Mazin, we contacted because he pointed out the tasks of the Medical Service to us often, but we didn't go into any other details of the military operations. We were constantly reminded to go about our tasks in a professional and responsible manner, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, is it fair to say that you were not an operative commander of the Special Police during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I was not an operative commander. I was a volunteer in the Medical Service. That's the rank of an assistant commander, but I was not a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I take it during Operation Storm, itself, you were never specifically or officially tasked by anyone with monitoring the movements or discipline of the Special Police units deployed in the field?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Those are military tasks. My tasks pertained exclusively to my profession and the Medical Service. I was familiar with certain tasks, but only for purposes of assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And generally with respect to your going through places like Mazin and travelling between Gracac and Donji Lapac, you mentioned today that -- at page 16 that the pace of events was fast. And then on page 17 of the draft transcript today, you were also asked about whether you had noticed individuals entering houses, looting, setting house on fire, criminal conduct, and that was with respect to when you moved towards Mazin. And your answer was that you can't testify to that because you never saw any of it, and you believed that was due to the pace of the movement of the advance. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You have to know, though, that there were breaks in between. I was only mentioning the advancement of the unit whose member I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I take it that your answer, in terms of not being able to testify to specifics when you were advancing, holds true for the entirety of the fast pace advance. So when you're moving from Gracac to Lapac, or you're moving from Gracac to Mazin and then through to Donji Lapac, that answer is true for all of those movements; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: If I had seen anything of the sort, I would have told you. Since I had not seen any of it, there's nothing I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And to be clear, your answer is that -- you're not saying it didn't happen; you're just saying that you didn't see it. Is that -- that's fair, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: With my unit, I didn't see or experience any of it. Had I, I would have shared it with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you said that you arrived in Gracac on the 5th of August. Do you know exactly when it was that you arrived in Gracac, like the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It is difficult to recall which day exactly, but I do seem to recall that it was sometime in the afternoon. It may have been 1.00 or 2.00 p.m., although I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And how long did you actually spend in Gracac, total?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I was in Gracac briefly only, because we withdrew towards a place called Stikada, I believe. We stayed there. I only went through Gracac on the main road. I was in the Health Centre for a short while, assessing whether our medical teams could be housed there. That's it. I saw, on the other side of the street, that there was a police station, and I saw several civilians there. I think I was there for only a brief period of time before we withdrew to the periphery of Gracac, I believe. It is in the outskirts, and I believe it is called Stikada. We were close to the lake there and the hydro-electric plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, similarly - I assume it's the same difficulty - do you know exactly when you arrived in Donji Lapac on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I can recall that it was -- excuse me, apologies. The dates are as stated in the statement, but I think I may have made an error. I think the operation started on the 4th rather than the 5th. On the 4th, we were at positions, so I may have made a mistake in terms of that one day. I don't know if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that we're clear. Is it that you're saying you could have arrived in Donji Lapac a day afterwards, or a day before, or you're not sure if it was the 7th or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: As you can find it in the statement, that is what I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, you gave your statement six months ago. Did you remember then or did you have something in front of you to help you remember? How did -- I'm just wondering why it is you can't remember today, but six months ago you were giving dates.

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Of course, it is more difficult to think straight in this situation because I'm on the stand for the first time in my life. Now you're asking me to tell you something that I am supposed to stand by. The giving of the statement took place under different circumstances than those of today. This is the first time I ever appeared as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Did you not have anything in front of you at the time to help you remember dates, or was anybody helping you with timing or dates when you were being interviewed, anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, no, I had no aids. I was trying to recall things and to be as precise as possible. I didn't think it was all that important, though. Your memories fade after a number of years, but you try to place it within a certain context or date. I was doing my utmost to basically forget about the war, since it was an ugly episode in my life. Whenever I tried to recall it, I experienced stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So with respect to Donji Lapac, irrespective of the time you arrived, do you know or do you have a sense of how long it was you actually stayed in Donji Lapac itself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: In Donji Lapac itself, we also spent a brief period of time. It was my belief that each of the operations were to take longer than the few days they did. I remember that we spent the night in the outskirts and another night immediately close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Herman, when you say "a brief period," are you talking perhaps one or two hours before you left; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: A day. It was my belief that the operation would take days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm trying to understand that. If you arrived in Donji Lapac, my understanding is that Donji Lapac wasn't freed until the afternoon on the 7th. So if you're saying you stayed a day, does that mean that you stayed overnight there, or you -- because you just said that you didn't stay overnight in the town, so it's clearly less than a day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We spent the night on the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So when you say "a brief period in Donji Lapac," you're talking about less than a day, perhaps a few hours; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: In the center of Donji Lapac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You've indicated today, at pages 18 to 19, that during the time that the HV entered the town, there was firing of weapons, which you considered dangerous, and you said you didn't really move about the area. So can you explain how much time elapsed between your entry into Donji Lapac and when you recall the HV coming into town and starting to fire weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It was a matter of a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And how long after the HV entered did you leave Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We withdrew as quickly as we could to the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So within one hour; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did with my group, that is. My task was to examine people and give them advice, because they were exhausted. I had some peace and quiet to do that. I don't know the area very well, but I do know that we were in a house where I had conversations with the members of my team. There were some problems they were experiencing, but they were minor and due to exhaustion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: In your statement, you noted that not a single member of the Special Police participated in activities that you're attributing to the HV when they entered Donji Lapac. I just want to know, are you referring to the celebration and the firing of weapons or are you referring to the burning and looting that occurred in Donji Lapac in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: We have to be on the same page here. I am referring to my own Varazdin unit. There's nothing else I can tell you about any other members. We withdrew to the outskirts once the celebration began. As for any burning, I didn't see any of our members do that, and I mean specifically the members of the Varazdin unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: At page 19 in today's draft transcript, you said that when you were withdrawing from Donji Lapac there were houses that had been set on fire. Did you see who set those houses on fire as you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, no. I saw that from a distance. I could see that some houses were in flames, although I can't tell you anything about who may have set them on fire. I didn't see that. I must say that I tried to influence the -- my members to the extent possible. I tried to explain to them why properties should not be burned, since it was the property of Croatian citizens. I tried to exercise my influence over the members of my unit. That was in my best interest, since I am fully aware of the importance of such things, and I placed great importance to the notion of a home, as such, as I do today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And during the brief period you were in Donji Lapac, did you notice any houses marked with the letters "HV" or houses marked with the letters "MUP," MUP?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I was in the field often, and I did see some similar things. However, I didn't see that in Lapac. It is difficult for me to tell you where I saw that. I went from Vukovar all the way to Dubrovnik, and I did see some signs like that. As far as I know, care was taken of houses in such a way because many places were mixed, in terms of population, and perhaps some Croats were trying to protect their own homes, although I'm not completely clear as to their motivation. To me, these are all Croatian homes and houses. A house is a house, no matter how you look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Doctor, I just want to return to one point here about how well you know General Markac. Could you give us a number, in terms of the total times you and General Markac have sat down together and had a meeting, a personal meeting between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to tell you any figure that would be close to the truth. I can tell you, though, that we had several conversations, and we covered different topics, such as sports, et cetera. He influenced me very positively, since I was a volunteer, because he placed great emphasis on equal treatment, irrespective of one's colour of skin, religious affiliation, or ethnic background. I particularly appreciated him for that because my life's vocation is to assist people, and I see myself as a humanitarian, valuing a human life.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Herman, you were asked by Mr. Mikulicic today to comment on your impressions of General Markac, and you've offered the opinion that he was moral, honourable, a patriot, and you described him as professional in his work. Moreover, in your statement you mention at a number of different points that General Markac insisted that, in essence, the Rules of War were to be complied with during Special Police operations, and you've said the same again today in court. Is that -- that's all accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If he were in command today, I believe he would still be insisting on the same issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Herman, can you imagine General Markac to be the type of commander that would consider falsely accusing the opposing military forces of having launched a sabotage attack or some other unjustified attack as a pretext in order to give the false impression that Croatian forces were provoked and, therefore, justified in launching a military action?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I take it, then, it would surprise you if General Markac considered creating such a pretext on one -- more than one occasion as the commander of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: That would surprise me very unpleasantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, finally, Dr. Herman, in terms of your evidence on General Markac's insistence that the rules be followed, et cetera, did you consider any instance or are you aware of any instance where General Markac had agreed to abide by certain rules or conditions, in order to gain a certain advantage, and later decided to unilaterally break those rules or conditions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I had no opportunity to see it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Herman. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Herman, you told us about a tank firing from this column. Could you give us any further details?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I was on that forest road that I mentioned. A shell was fired in the direction of that area. Those tanks were leaving the town. I could see that they joined the civilian column, which was inconceivable by my standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us exactly where you were at that moment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: That is difficult to say. It was as one is leaving the forested area and entering the residential area. I must say that I was quite terrified when I heard the sound of a tank. I can freely confess that tanks cause fear in me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see the tank firing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see the shell landing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. It landed somewhere in the forest, but I could clearly hear the explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it one shell or were there more?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: There was one specific shell for which I believed was a tank shell. Otherwise, several shells landed not on top of our heads, but in the forest itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another question is about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the person who interviewed you. Let me just find it. One second, please. You said that you were interviewed by -- that Djurica Franjo was present during your interview. Now, from a hierarchical structure, so I'm not talking about whether you ever received orders from him, but hierarchically was he at a higher level than you were in the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN HERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know that he served with the MUP for a great many years. There's nothing else I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions triggered by the questions by the Bench? Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Herman, in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming and for answering questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Herman out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some time left for procedural matters. I would like to start with the guidance for the presentation of agreed facts. The Chamber will now delivery its guidance on the presentation of agreed facts between the parties. On the 2nd of October, 2009, the Cermak Defence filed six motions requesting the Chamber to admit evidence under Rule 92 bis of the Rules and one motion to admit evidence under Rule 92 quater of the Rules, totalling nearly 1.400 pages in combined length. On the 9th of October, the Chamber, considering the nature and the scope of the matters that the Cermak Defence apparently wished to demonstrate with the extensive 92 bis and quater material tendered, indicated that the Cermak Defence should seek other avenues for the material's admission. The Chamber indicated that in the circumstances at hand, the most appropriate manner for the material to be presented would be through agreed facts, and subsequently invited the parties to come to an agreement. All of this can be found at transcript pages 22.866 to 22.870. On the 10th of November, the Cermak Defence informed the Chamber that, together with the Prosecution, it was producing a single document with agreed facts between the parties covering both the Rule 92 bis and 92 quater material. This can be found at transcript pages 24.461 to 24.464. Subsequently, on the 18th of November, the parties informed the Chamber that in spite of having come to an agreement on the facts, the manner in which these facts should be presented to the Chamber remained in dispute. The Cermak Defence and the Gotovina Defence argued that the agreed facts should be formally admitted into evidence, while the Prosecution took the position that the agreed facts should only be taken notice of by the Chamber, without such formal admission into evidence. This can be found on transcript pages 24.729 through 24.741. Rule 65 ter (H) states: "The Pre-Trial Judge shall record the points of agreement and disagreement on matters of law and fact. In this connection, he or she may order the parties to file written submissions with either the Pre-Trial Judge or the Trial Chamber." Rule 65 ter (M) allows a Trial Chamber to exercise proprio motu any of the functions of the Pre-Trial Judge. Regarding points of agreement, material presented through a joint filing of the parties will be part of the trial record on which the parties can rely in future submissions. An agreement on matters of fact removes these facts from the area of dispute between the parties and will make it highly unlikely that any of them will present evidence to the contrary of what was agreed upon. Similarly, reasons for not excepting the agreed facts for the truth of their content are unlikely to be found by a Chamber when making its final findings. The Chamber may rely on these facts for the truth of their content without any additional evidence presented in relation to them. However, the Chamber is not bound by any point of fact or law agreed upon between the parties and recorded in a filing under Rule 65 ter (H) of the Rules. The ultimate weight of these agreed facts will be determined by the totality of the evidence. As to the question of whether agreed facts have to be formally admitted, the parties refer to a number of decisions in support of their respective positions. In the case of Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and Jokic, the Trial Chamber, on the 19th of December, 2003, clarified that the recording of points of agreement during the trial phase results in the acceptance of those agreed points as evidence under Rule 89(C) of the Rules. This holding was confirmed by the Trial Chambers in the cases of Prosecutor versus Halilovic on the 25th of July, 2005, and Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic on the 10th of April, 2007. This Chamber then considers that whether or not a separate decision on admission is taken, the status of the agreed facts which are recorded is not any less than evidence formally tendered and admitted under Rule 89(C) of the Rules. Considering this case law, the Chamber finds that formal admission of the agreed facts and assigning these facts an exhibit number would constitute an unnecessary procedural step. The Chamber does not, in adjudicating the cases before it, distinguish between the status of points of fact the parties have agreed upon which were recorded in a joint filing and points of fact agreed upon by the parties which were submitted for a decision on admission under Rule 89(C) of the Rules. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber requests that the parties submit their table of agreed facts in the form of a joint filing. Further, the Chamber requests the Cermak Defence to withdraw the outstanding Rule 92 bis and quater motions covered by the joint filing. And this concludes the Chamber's guidance on the presentation of agreed facts. Are there any other procedural matters the parties would like to address at this moment, apart from the one I mentioned earlier, because this Friday is the last Friday before the recess, and while a clean table is perhaps too much to be wished, but at least as clean as possible. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've never been very good at washing up after being at the table, Your Honour, but we do ask indulgence in relation to this agreed facts matter because the parties will have to meet to sign it. And we ask that that be done after the recess, for logistical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will miss it over the recess, but we know approximately what it is about. And, of course, the Chamber has earlier looked at the 92 bis and 92 quater motions, so the Chamber has at least a slight idea of what it may expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Something to look forward to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you were on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Just briefly, Mr. President. I believe in past recesses, the Chamber has expanded the time in which to either file or respond to motions should any party file them during this period of time. We haven't discussed that with the Prosecution, but we have done that both in the summer recess, I believe, and last Christmas's recess. So I do think we can come to some resolution, and -- so come to a resolution on timing so no one feels they have to come back from vacation to file any responses. But I think we can agree to that outside of court and just provide Chambers with what our agreement is for ultimate determination. And I think that the Chambers -- Mr. President has given us the Chamber's conclusion informally. I don't think anybody would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, we are a bit in a different position. We are coming closer and closer to the end of the case presentation. And before committing the Chamber to an agreement reached by the parties, the Chamber would like to review what pending motions there are and whether they would all allow for such a delay. Not to say that the Chamber will not support and adopt any suggestion by the parties, but at this stage of the proceedings I'd like to be a bit more cautious in already granting definitive effect to such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Mikulicic, the other issue. Would you prefer to have a break before you respond? Because let me tell you what apparently seems to be the situation. I leave aside for this moment issues like responses filed late, or I also leave aside for the time being, not to say that it is totally irrelevant, but the timing of the motion or whether good cause has been shown to introduce this matter at this moment. I would like you primarily to focus on some of the objections raised by the Prosecution, once the Prosecution -- once you had filed the expert report of Mr. Watts. By the way, it was not filed as an expert report, but it was filed as a report in your second filing explaining and giving information to the Prosecution on what they could expect as far as relevance is concerned.
