It seems to be a -- there are a few matters apparently raised by the Prosecution, the first being that most -- at least half of the expert report of Mr. Watts is purely of a legal nature, that is, to explain the law. Mr. Watts, in the report, as we've seen, analyses what the case law of this Tribunal tells us. Not to say that legal expertise is, under all circumstances, excluded, but you may remember that the Chamber has ruled on, for example, the expert report of Mr. Corn and has said something about legal expertise. The second part of the report analyses the liability of Mr. Markac under the theory of superior responsibility. One of the concerns expressed by the Prosecution is that Mr. Watts relies considerably on statements to which the Chamber has no access. The Sacic statement, I think, is footnoted at 10 instances. I refer you to paragraph 54 of the report. And we see in the following parts of the report that the knowledge of Mr. Markac plays an important role. For example, in paragraph 69 of the report we find the knowledge of Mr. Markac to be of importance for drawing further conclusions. The Chamber has no statement of Mr. Sacic, and it was argued by the Prosecution that it would be inadmissible evidence because it was a statement taken for the purposes of this Tribunal which would not be admissible under Rule 92 ter -- 92 bis, 92 ter, or 92 quater. As far as access to a statement and even potential testimony, the Chamber has no access to it. And the situation certainly would not have been improved over the last one day and a half. The report gives rather far-reaching conclusions. On the basis of this material, the expert reaches conclusions such as: Based on the rules under which Markac operated, and according to the expert's knowledge and expertise, in the doctrine of superior responsibility, it is his opinion that Markac did not commit sufficiently culpable omissions to impose criminal liability for events at Grubori, which is at least a statement which is at risk to do what the Chamber has to do. And then again apparently Mr. Watts bases his opinion, among other matters, but certainly in a rather important aspect, on material which is not accessible for the Chamber. The Chamber would like you to specifically address these matters, not excluding you from any other matters, in 10 minutes. And whether you'd like to do it now or to do it after the break, I leave that to you. I would -- of course, the matter came up only in the second round of exchange of views, and that's the reason why the Chamber exceptionally would like to hear brief oral submissions on specifically these matters. The Chamber is also aware that, of course, we have two stages. The first is to add a witness to the 65 ter list; and, of course, the second issue, but not totally unrelated, the admission of evidence as an expert report as presented as an annex to your submissions seeking to have the 65 ter list amended and Mr. Watts being added. Would you like to do it before the break or after the break? As I said before, the Chamber has in mind certainly not more than 10 minutes at this stage, and the Chamber would allow a brief response then for the Prosecution - you were the moving party - but also certainly not more than six, seven, eight minutes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would very much prefer to do it after the break. I found myself in a rather peculiar position because this is the matter dealt with by my co-counsel, Mr. Kuzmanovic, and legal assistant, Mr. David Gault. They both are absent now, and I'm not quite familiar with the matters that -- in such details that you just introduced. So I will consult with my colleagues during the break, and I will try to give you a satisfactory answer afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You will understand that, I think, the original motion was filed the 11th of November. The Prosecution responded on the 26th of November. Then the Defence replied on the 4th of December. And the Prosecution then sur-replied the 11th of December. So, therefore, the Chamber doesn't want to -- I think it would not be good to wait until after the recess, because that would disturb substantially your scheduling of witnesses; at least it may have an impact on that. And, therefore, the Chamber would rather already decide the matter, even if there's not yet a full written decision, preferably today or in the few days to come so that you have practical guidance. And that's the reason why we asked you to make further submissions. We'll do that after the break. If you need a bit of a longer break in order to be better able to consult with -- I don't know where Mr. Kuzmanovic is. I hope he's not back in the States, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is. He's somewhere over the ocean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be early in the morning for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would suggest, with your permission and your guidance, I would suggest that until Monday, so over the weekend, we could produce written answers to your remarks, and we could file it on Monday. So within three days, counting the weekend between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have considered your request, and the Chamber will not allow you to wait until after the weekend. That causes all kind of huge logistical problems. You more or less triggered the difficulty by a relatively late filing. I'm not anticipating on a decision on whether the filing was too late or not, but at least it was on the 11th of November, and then the report became available only as an annex to your filing on the 4th of December. The Chamber, nevertheless, wants to accommodate you in some respect; that is, that if you'd prefer to make a written filing, you would have until 5.00 today to do that, even if it's not formally filed, but if a courtesy copy is given to the Chamber, that will do, which allows the Chamber to deal with this matter in a meeting to take place later today. And the Judges are not able to meet after the weekend, because we'll all be at different locations, and these are matters which are in need of a thorough discussion, rather than a phone call of five or ten minutes, apart from whether that could be organised. Further, the Chamber also considers it important that you receive the guidance you need. Therefore, the Chamber leaves it to you, Mr. Mikulicic. You also could do both. If you say, Let me consult with -- I don't know, you said is he above the ocean or at the other side of the ocean already?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Above the ocean, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Above the ocean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think his flight started at 10.30 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that you -- I don't know whether you can reach him. I know that there is some communication possible sometimes from planes as well, but I leave it in your hands. If -- do you know what the arrival time of the plane is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say eight hours from starting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes it's six, seven, eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So I believe it's -- let me count. I'm not very good in mathematics, Your Honour. So it will be ten and six. It will be like 4.00 in the afternoon, something like this, our time counting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As someone who also takes the Amsterdam to Chicago flight quite frequently, I think 4.00 is a bit hopeful. I would suspect it's past 6.00 our time here that he would arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you -- I wouldn't say "flight attendant" for this information, but at least thank you for this information. One second. I'm just checking my e-mail at this moment on the proposed practicalities of further meetings with the Republic of Croatia. The Prosecution has asked for a third person to be present. So has the Gotovina Defence. We'll look at what is possible. We have to find an accommodation which provides for everything. We need this interpretation, possibly transcript. One final matter which I would like to ask the parties about. If we would meet with the Republic of Croatia, it would not be part of a court hearing; it would be a preparatory meeting. The Prosecution has suggested that a transcript be made. Now, one of the issues brought to our attention by the Registry was that it might be difficult to have French translation available which is, of course, needed, if a transcript in French would have to be prepared as well. I'm seeking the position of the parties as to limiting this non-formal court hearing if the Chamber would decide that immediately, simultaneously, a transcript would be made, that we would not insist on a French interpreter being there. So that also dis-enables to have a French transcript made at any later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the view of the Gotovina Defence team is we don't need a transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider it. The Chamber suggested, I think, an audio recording, so that if need be, a transcript could be made at a later stage. Mr. Waespi, would you explain why you find it of such importance already to have immediately a transcript being made?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think that's for the benefit of all the participants at that meeting. As you know, it's usually good to see what people have said previously. But I can go back to Mr. Tieger and then ask for his specific reason. I'm sure that the transcript in French is not an issue at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. I suggest the following: The Chamber would like to consider how to proceed with -- whether we should first inquire as to whether Mr. Kuzmanovic has a tail wind or head wind, and what is still possible for the Chamber. As I said before, these are matters the Judges want to discuss and not to exchange brief e-mails on these matters. I suggest that we have a break, that you further inquire as to at what moment Mr. Kuzmanovic will switch his mobile phone on again, how much time you'd need. We'll also need to have a look at, perhaps, what the possibilities are for the Chamber to meet. But the urgency of the matter is something that was not triggered by the Chamber. I suggest that we -- since we might not need to discuss any other matter, that perhaps we take a bit of a longer break. Mr. Mikulicic, if you would see no possibilities at all to make further submissions in writing today, you might want to prepare for brief oral submissions. In view of the time-limits the Chamber sets, we'll have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the state of affairs, more or less: When we take into account Mr. Watts' expertise, without going into the details that you pointed out, but bearing those in mind nonetheless, when we put it in the context of these new developments, so to say, in Croatia, which will most likely result in a number of new facts specifically related to the Grubori events, being one of the central parts of the indictment, then I believe that submitting an expert report in the absence of information to be obtained by virtue of these new developments would, in any case, be premature. That is why, Your Honour, this Defence is in favour of withdrawing putting Mr. Watts, the expert witness, on the 65 ter list, and to exclude his expert testimony from our Defence case. In other words, we withdraw all our requests pertaining to that. As I have already stated in the morning, in view of the new developments, we reserve the right to react to any new developments of what may ensue in Croatia and the procedure that is underway there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the other Defence teams have no submissions to make on this matter? Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Irrespective of whether the Chamber can adopt the reasons why, it is on the record that the request to amend the 65 ter list has been withdrawn, and that is where it stands now. It's put on the record. That is clear. A final matter. Have the parties discussed the extension of time for any pending motions, and what would be their suggestions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I spoke to Mr. Waespi, and we're just going to go back and look at our e-mail traffic from last Christmas, and I was going to consult with him and then forward that to the Chamber. We have not done a specific time-frame or haven't given a specific time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber, of course, will have to decide rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there will be any e-mails which express any joint position, we'll, of course, consider them, which is not the same as to accept any joint position by the two parties. But we will consider that. If you would like to have a fair chance that the Chamber will have a look at it, then it's advised to wait not longer than until 3.00 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I have just one minute to talk to Mr. Waespi across the divide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the agreement of the parties was, as opposed to the two weeks that is in the Rules, three weeks from the date of any filing. I understand Your Honour has timing concerns, but in order to accommodate everybody's schedule, that's what the parties agreed to. And we make that proposal jointly to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just a couple of points. The only filing -- the two filings we will obviously comply with is the dead-line of today. I think there is one on Tuesday, our response to the request for certification to the Appeals Chamber. And that, of course, isn't affected by any agreement. And just another additional point to what we were discussing before the break in relation to this preparatory meeting. The record the Prosecution suggests to have is not a simultaneous record, as we have it now, but just any record like it's usually done after the 65 ter meetings, which is usually available, I think, the day after the meeting. That would be sufficient from the Prosecution's perspective. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that matter. There may be technical possibilities to do that. Otherwise, we have to find another way of recording, because most important would be where there is agreement and where there is no agreement. And we'll certainly -- if not through a verbatim transcript, there will certainly be ways found to avoid whatever confusion or mal-communication. The Chamber will further consider the matter. Any other matter on the table? If not, we will then adjourn, but we'll not do so without having wished everyone -- whether Christmas is in December or whether Christmas is in early January, we wish everyone the very best for those -- for Christmas and for the new year to come. The Chamber is aware that we are not all in the same position. The Chamber is aware that it is -- especially in detention, it's harder to enjoy these days. Nevertheless, the Chamber wants to wish -- to give the best wishes for these days to everyone in this courtroom and those just outside the courtroom assisting us. We adjourn, and we resume on Monday, the 11th of January, 2010, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
